ai.definition: Digital Afterlife is the theoretical concept of transferring an individual's consciousness or mind into a digital environment, allowing for continued existence after physical death.
ai.howItWorks: The process involves mapping and replicating neural patterns to simulate conscious experiences in artificial systems. This requires advanced neuroscanning technologies capable of capturing intricate brain activity and translating it into computational models that can be hosted on digital platforms.
ai.problemSolved: Preserving consciousness posthumously and extending the existence of individuals beyond physical death.
ai.manufacturing: Highly speculative; currently no known technology exists to achieve this. It would require breakthroughs in neuroscanning, AI, and quantum computing.
ai.buildProcess: Involves developing ultra-high-resolution brain scanning techniques, creating algorithms capable of interpreting neural data, and integrating these with advanced AI systems for simulation.
ai.costDrivers: Extremely high due to the cutting-edge nature of required technologies; potential costs could range from billions to trillions of dollars per individual, depending on the level of detail and sophistication desired.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The concept is in its infancy with no clear path to commercialization. Significant technological and ethical hurdles must be overcome before it can become a reality.
ai.regulation: Currently unregulated; however, as the technology advances, regulatory frameworks will need to be established to address privacy, consent, and ethical concerns.
ai.risks: High risk due to unknowns in neurobiology, AI ethics, data security, and potential loss of identity or consciousness. There are also significant legal and social implications that have yet to be fully understood.
ai.profitability: Not commercially viable at present; speculative and unproven technology with no clear market demand or business model.
ai.futureDevelopment: Potential for breakthroughs in AI, neuroscanning, and quantum computing could make the concept more feasible. However, it remains a distant possibility without substantial advancements.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units would draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking and complex computational requirements.

glossary.def: The specific electrical activity within the brain that corresponds to conscious experiences.
The state of being aware and having subjective experiences.
Computational environments designed to simulate human-like cognitive processes.

subsystems.name: Preservation and fixation
subsystems.role: stops decay so the brain's structure can be read out later.

subsystems.name: Volumetric imaging
subsystems.role: captures every neuron, process and synapse at nanometre resolution.

subsystems.name: Reconstruction pipeline
subsystems.role: stitches terabytes of images into a coherent three-dimensional volume.

subsystems.name: Connectome and cell atlas
subsystems.role: the wiring diagram plus the identity and properties of each cell type.
parts: graph database of neurons and synapses

subsystems.name: Neuron and network models
subsystems.role: turns a static wiring diagram into something that transmits signals in time.
parts: simulation engine and neuromorphic or GPU hardware

subsystems.name: Embodiment and interface
subsystems.role: gives the simulated network inputs, outputs and an environment to act in.
parts: output decoding to speech or control

buildSteps.title: Stabilise the tissue
buildSteps.detail: The brain is chemically fixed or vitrified within minutes of death so that synaptic structure is not lost to decay.

buildSteps.title: Cut and image
buildSteps.detail: The volume is sliced or milled away a few nanometres at a time while an electron microscope photographs each newly exposed face.

buildSteps.title: Reconstruct the volume
buildSteps.detail: Software aligns the millions of images and traces every membrane, producing a labelled map of cells and synapses.

buildSteps.title: Extract the connectome
buildSteps.detail: The traced cells are turned into a graph of which neuron connects to which, where, and with what size of contact.

buildSteps.title: Assign cell types and properties
buildSteps.detail: Expression data and electrode recordings say whether each cell excites or inhibits, and how it responds to input.

buildSteps.title: Build the simulation
buildSteps.detail: The graph and cell models are loaded onto a supercomputer or neuromorphic chip and run in real time.

buildSteps.title: Close the loop with an interface
buildSteps.detail: Inputs are fed in from a simulated or real environment, and the network's output is decoded back out.

buildSteps.title: Validate against behaviour
buildSteps.detail: The simulation is only credible if it reproduces the responses the original brain gave.

prerequisites.why: whole brains of a worm and a fly have been mapped; a human brain is roughly a million times larger.
humans cannot trace billions of neurons by hand, and automatic tracing still needs heavy proofreading.
simulating tens of billions of neurons with detailed dynamics is at or beyond the top of today's machines.

prerequisites.tech: A validated theory linking structure to experience
prerequisites.why: nobody has shown that a correct wiring diagram, run on a computer, produces the same mind.
current fixation and vitrification methods destroy the tissue they preserve.

pathway.milestone: complete wiring maps of small nervous systems and small patches of mammalian cortex
pathway.unlocks: proof that connectome-scale reconstruction is possible at all.

pathway.milestone: whole mouse brain emulation that reproduces measurable behaviours
pathway.unlocks: a test case where the result can be checked against the living animal.

pathway.milestone: non-destructive, high-resolution scanning of a living or recoverable brain
pathway.unlocks: removes the need to destroy the person to read them.

pathway.milestone: human-scale emulation with a tested account of consciousness
pathway.unlocks: the only version of a 'digital afterlife' that would mean anything — and it remains unproven.
